utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin is continuing with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning to you and Your Honours, and everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, at the end of yesterday's session, we were looking at a document, and I'd like to carry on with some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: So I would ask if we could have, again, P1434 on the screen and for the first page of that document to be showing, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, let me know if you need have this blown up any more, but, I think, for the moment it helps to see the layout of the page. Again, this is a VRS document we saw yesterday, signed by Captain Zoran Cakic and sent on the 30th of July of 1995. And sir, you can see, starting in the middle of the page, a list of names. It says: "Information about r/z ... in the holding centre Rogatica. "Since 28 July 1995 the following Muslims have a status of prisoners of war placed in the military holding centre in Rogatica."

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you look down that list of names, please. And, first of all, look at the person at number 5. Tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And the information given there has your name, the year of your birth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And it lists you as wounded. Now, the other names on the list, starting from the top, can you go and look down this list and tell us if these were the people who were with you in the Rasadnik prison camp. Starting with Mr. Hajric, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the people on the list were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, just to pick out the highlights there, we have at number 1, Mehmed Hajric. Year of birth is given as 1968. A former president of the War Presidency of the Zepa SOQ, a hodza by profession. Number 2, we have Hamdija Torlak. Number 3, Amir Imamovic. And we've heard about them from you already yesterday, sir. Can we see the next page, please. And you will see that the list continues, sir. If you could continue to look down the list and tell us if those people also were with you in the Rasadnik prison camp.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the person under number 45. It says Atlantida, 1058. I don't know him. But as for the others, yes, I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could actually show the full width of the text at number 45 there just so you can read with what it says. And there it says after Atlantida, and the number, "in the safe place and at another location." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: According to the numbering on list, there were 44 prisoners in the camp at the time this report was written. Does that match your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Yesterday we said that from Tisca there was a total of 43 persons who were returned. One day following our arrival, Huso Cocalic joined us as the 44th person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I think that we'll see just on the list here between numbers 32 and then 34, there appears to be some kind of gap. And, unfortunately, we don't have the original paper copy of this document, but there appears to be some gap there, and I just wanted to raise that for the record. But the numbering continues, 32, 34, and then goes through here, up until 45 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And I think at the bottom, we can see the letter C as a heading. If we could try to zoom in on that part of the screen. Sir, let me know if you can read the text at point C. If necessary, I can give you a hard copy of that page if it is not possible to read the text with that width.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. And I hope that's okay for the Defence as well. We can read there that it says: "Pursuant to the orders and instructions of General Tolimir, all the necessary measures are taken and in accordance to the possibility they are mainly being carried out. Among other things the following was done: "Categorisation of r/z was done and they are placed in three rooms: the healthy in one room, the wounded and the sick in another room, and the members of the former leadership in the third room." Does this correspond with how you were accommodated in the prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded and sick were placed in two small rooms that were adjacent to each other. One could move between the two rooms, so we could say that they were basically in the same room. The rest is as it is stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When it refers to the members of the former leadership being in a third room, do you know who that refers to?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hamdija Torlak, Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you know for how long those three men were together in a room?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not certain. But up to two weeks, maximum, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And after that point, where were they accommodated or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Imamovic and Mehmed Hajric, we simply stopped seeing them. Until that time, we were taken out for walks together in front of the prison building. On one occasion, we were taken all together to the river to take a bath there, which was about a kilometre away. After we stopped seeing them, I don't know what fate they met, or where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, next in this document it says: "Atlantida is separated and placed at another location and has better accommodation." You have already told us you don't know anything about this Atlantida. So I will read on. Then it says: "The effendi is allowed to pray in the room five times a day." Do you know who the "effendi" here refers to?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could this refer to anyone else except for Mr. Hajric? In this context, in the camp here, not in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it does refer to anyone else. The word "effendi" tells you that he was a hodza. It was approved to him to carry out religious rites five times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, since we talked about the three men who were referred to as hodza in Zepa yesterday, just to be clear, do you know if either of the other two men who you told us about yesterday were in the Rasadnik prison camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now, it says: "They have food (three times a day) - they use an outhouse." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you use this outhouse, toilet, freely, when you wanted?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning and in the evening, we went as a group. We were taken out of the prison building and then we would have to line up four at a time to go and use the toilet. In between those times, if needed, they allowed us to go, when we had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Was there anything else you had to do when you were lined up and going to use the facilities?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. They forced us to sing Chetnik songs as of the moment we would leave the building en route to the toilet, and while we were in the toilet, as well as on our way back. Along the route, there were always three military policemen: one at the corner of the building where we started; another one halfway to the toilet; and the third in front of the toilet itself, to guard us. If someone refused to sing, they would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Then it says in the document: "They have medical treatment." Did you receive medical treatment for your leg injuries while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon arrival, we were visited by their doctors. They bandaged our wounds and assisted us. A few days later, ICRC physicians visited us. They did much the same thing, but that was the extent of any medical assistance. There was one sick person, though, who had leg problems who was taken to Sokolac, I believe, to the hospital there. First, he had his toes cut off, and, later on, immediately before the exchange, he was taken there again. They amputated his left or right lower leg; I'm not sure which.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you didn't receive regular medical treatment from a doctor, were you able to look after your wounds yourself?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I had enough medical supplies in my bag. Of course, all those items were taken away and placed in one of the rooms. But since I personally knew the deputy camp warden because we were in the same class at school for three years, I asked him a few times to give me the supplies so that I could bandage my wounds. He categorically refused. Since there was a lot of puss and oozing from the wound, I used toilet paper to collect that. I received that toilet paper from the ICRC. In other words, I had no medical supplies that I could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Finally, right at the bottom of the page, it says: "On 30th of July this year, the r/z are visited and registered by ICRC delegation - office at Pale." Is this the visit you told us about by the ICRC shortly after you arrived at Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to see, please, now 65 ter 2240. I'd ask Your Honours if this could not be broadcast. It's an ICRC document, and our usual practice is to try to preserve ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could see page 1 in the B/C/S, and I think the corresponding page in English is page 2, since there's a cover letter that appears in the sequence of documents there. I'd like that. We should see the same page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the heading here is: "Working paper on ICRC visit to Rogatica War Admission Camp, 30.07 and 31.07.1995." And if you look down, sir, to the paragraph numbered 1 which is currently at the bottom of the screen, it says: "Progress of the visit. The ICRC delegates had been granted free access to 44 detainees in total. Thirty-two were visited for the first time and were registered. The other 12 were already registered ... on July 26, 1995." You've told us you remember the Red Cross visiting. Do you remember if there were visits on two consecutive days, as is indicated by this document?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They came one day and registered those who had not been registered previously. The next day ICRC physicians arrived, and I presume they came to see the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for the document to be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2240 shall be assigned Exhibit P2251, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to hear from you now your story about what was happening in the camp, particularly starting through the days -- we've heard about your first days of arrival but from the beginning of August of 1995. What was happening, who did you see, how were people being treated?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first fortnight or the first ten days upon arrival, there were basically no activities in the camp. Once a day, we were taken out for some 40 minutes, up to one hour, for a walk in front of the prison building. We walked in a circle lined up in a column. The whole time we had to sing Chetnik songs. Usually towards the evening when those in charge left the camp, and I primarily mean the prison warden, the beatings started, depending on who was on guard that evening. In a shift, we would spend a quiet night and then in another shift, the beatings basically never stopped. They would barge into the room, take out, beat people, return them, either one by one or in groups. Following those first ten days, they started taking us to perform work obligation. First they took out older people and then those who were wounded, depending on their health situation. At the same time, the number of provocations and beatings diminished. We mainly went to work to the local sawmill in the town itself. I don't know how many people performed that work obligation specifically. We also went to cut wood for the command of their brigade. We had to provide firewood. In early October, we began going to Zepa to go to such buildings that had not been destroyed or burnt down. We took down all carpentry, timber that we could find, and we took it up to Borike where we managed to put together nine weekend homes. Three of them were regular-sized houses, and the other six were bungalow type. While we were constructing those buildings, another group continued being taken to Zepa, and they brought in hay that had been prepared by the population during the summer for their cattle. They also collected any wiring. In other words, anything that was left preserved, was then brought to Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And, sir, you said you were on work duty then in October in Zepa, as well as at Borike. Whereabouts did you go in Zepa on this work detail?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation has come back, so I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. Then we will see if that will be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to the centre of Zepa, where I took part in the removal of carpentry from the school building that had been built. The Ukrainian Battalion had been placed in the building during the war, and the children did not attend school at the time. That's why a new school was being built. It is that building that we stripped off timber. We also went to a number of weekend homes that had not been destroyed. We dismantled them and took them to Borike. Two of them were in the centre of Zepa and another was in Slap close to the place where the Zepa river flows into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, having been in Zepa last on the 27th of July of 1995, how did it look when you returned there for these work duties in October?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked totally different. Before we left Zepa, most of the buildings were, if not in good condition because they had been shelled before, but one could live in them. When I came in Zepa on the 8th of October, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: States the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I could see that most of the buildings were destroyed. Some were destroyed by explosives, while others were torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps can you see it already, but in the interpretation we've got a reference to: "When I came in Zepa on the 8th of October, 1992 ... I could see that most of the buildings were destroyed." Are you talking, sir, about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, about 1992. My first visit took place, I think, on the 8th of October, 1992, when they took us to bring over the construction materials which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you, I think you must be talking about 1995, if we're talking about the time [Overlapping speakers] ... in the prison camp.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do you agree with that, it's 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, 1995. October 1995, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You said some of the buildings appeared to have been destroyed by explosives while others had been torched. Do you remember any particular buildings that appeared to have been destroyed by explosives?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The local mosque was blown up, and one side building that was the so-called Vakuf building, as they called it, in the immediate vicinity of the mosque had business premises on the first floor, and there were three apartments on the second floor. That was also destroyed with the use of explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Are you aware of any of the Muslim residents of Zepa burning their own property or homes before they left in the evacuation in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I do not know that that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've already seen aerial images together in a combined exhibit of several before and after aerial shots from July and August of 1995, which is Exhibit P2178. I'd like to have that on the screen to use with this witness. Your Honours, to facilitate using that exhibit, we've put together a hard copy which is one of these A3 photo binders that has the six aerial shots showing on each double page the before and after of the same area. The only addition is that we have a layout that shows you how the images fit together, and I would ask if I could hand this out to Your Honours and also to the witness, simply to facilitate using Exhibit P2178. The witness has already seen it in proofing, and we've given copies to the Defence and also for the Bench and for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Please provide a copy to the -- to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just allowing the Defence to see the copy to be given to the witness, to be sure that it's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the content of this exhibit, it's -- the underlying images are those we were provided from the aerial image provider. But the layout and how we've put it together, that's the OTP's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, while you're looking, if you could open up the book and just look through the pages there. If you take a minute to orientate yourself you can see on the first page, you will see a combined set of images which shows the three images of the pages that follow. And hopefully you can see in the top right image marked number 3, the area of the centre of Zepa. And let me know if you're familiar with that orientation. And while we're looking at the hard copy, if we could have on the screen, I think, page number 5 of the electronic image. It should be showing the centre of Zepa on the 27th of July of 1995. Sir, the image on screen now, if you turn through the book to page 3 and to the yellow marking of page 3. So if you turn a couple of pages onwards from where you are. I think one more page. And then on the left of the double spread, the yellow number 3, we have the image that's on the screen. This is a shot of Zepa from the 27th of July, 1995. Again, to orientate you, we have indicated in a square in the middle of that page and with a label the central mosque. And do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And for your own orientation, do you see the area of the Zepa school where the Ukrainian compound was?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left of the building which we just mentioned; that is to say, the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And can you see on this image any of the locations you've told us about so far during your testimony, including -- let's start with the police station where you said -- or the building where the police office where you worked was located. Is that shown on this image?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that to the right from the facility which is in the square; that is to say, to the right of the mosque. It is a square building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think if you are able to work with this image, it might help then to mark this image with some of those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And ask if the usher could assist with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, the usher should assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the usher will come to help. As I mentioned in our meeting previously, then we can do this using the electronic pen. Perhaps we could start, if you could make an X mark and the number 1 next to it for the building where the police office was located.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Now could you mark the -- where you said the Ukrainian compound was, where you were before leaving from Zepa on the bus. And make an X and a number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if you're able to do it, could you make a mark, perhaps a circle to distinguish it for -- the place where you say you last saw Avdo Palic when you were leaving Zepa. And put a 3 next to the mark you make.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Also, sir, I don't know if you can do it based on the roads we can see leading off this image, but you said that your family, your parents' home was about 4 kilometres away. If you could put an arrow, if possible, showing in which direction that home was, that would also help us orientate.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the road, leading from the centre to the north, and the arrow points further in that direction, as I have marked it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Okay. That's great. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask if we could have the image saved and if we could have that admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This aerial photograph with the markings of the witness will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 5 of the Exhibit P2178 marked by the witness in court shall be assigned Exhibit P2252. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page now in e-court. And in the hard copy books, it's the page blue number 3 opposite on the same open spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, this is an image from the 24th of August of 1995. And, again, I hope you recognise the layout of the Zepa town. It is the same orientation as the previous image. Can you see the location of the mosque and the school in this image?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque remains in the same square in which it was, though the building does not exist anymore. And the outhouse, the Vakuf house in front of it, and the school remained in the same place where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the white squares marked around -- that we can see on this screen are indicated as buildings that have been destroyed. Does this extent of the destruction correspond with what you saw when you were in Zepa on your work detail at the beginning of October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These were privately owned family houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Had those privately owned family houses been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When your family returned to Zepa -- let's start -- When did your family return to Zepa, your parents?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned in the summer of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: When they returned, what was the condition of their house?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the first floor of the house was built in stone, that was the only part that remained. It couldn't burn, and that was saved. Everything else was destroyed, and so were all the outhouses. Everything had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And what about the property of other families in the area where your parents live? What was the condition of the houses of those other families?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the neighbours, all but one house had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think you also mentioned that on the work detail in Zepa, you went down to Slap, down by the river where the Drina river and the Zepa river meet. Did you observe the condition of any buildings as you travelled down to that location, or when you arrived at that location in October of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was just one weekend cottage in a normal condition. And I suppose this was the only reason for us to go there, to take it apart, and transport everything to Borike. As for other buildings, I didn't notice that any of them were still useable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you see what had been done to those other buildings, if anything? Were they simply unusable or had they been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were destroyed or, more specifically, torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Apart from the people who were with you on your work detail, did you see anybody in Zepa when you went there in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the local population, no one had remained there. Everybody had left Zepa. There were just two localities, one in the centre of Zepa where I saw a group of soldiers. I cannot be precise, perhaps 10 to 15 at the most, and in Slap at the check-point of the Ukrainian Battalion, there were five to six men there. I don't think there was anyone elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll ask just for the record you referred to soldiers at one location in Zepa and some men at a Ukrainian check-point in Slap. Who were those soldiers or those men? What -- what nationality or what organisation were they from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these were members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We're finished with that exhibit, so I won't ask you look at that anymore. Turn back briefly to what you were telling us about the goings-on at Rasadnik. You mentioned when you spoke yesterday a place you called, I think, the notorious room or the infamous room. Can you tell us about that? What was this room? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room was on the north side of the facility in which we were accommodated, but it had a separate entrance on the same northern side. It was physically separated by a single wall from the room in which I was accommodated, and throughout my stay at the camp, we knew that there was someone there. We always knew the numbers on the basis of the meals which were taken from the room where we had our lunch and dinner. But we didn't know who were the persons in question because we never had a chance to see anyone of them until the last visit by the Red Cross on the 11th of January, 1996. That was when they took three unregistered prisoners from that room and joined them with us practically for the first time and registered them. But during my previous stay, sometimes they would bring five meals for lunch, sometimes three, sometimes four. So practically we always knew what was the number of people there, but we didn't know who they were. And we called it the infamous room because 90 per cent of the time that someone spent there, there was torture, beatings. One could hear cries, screams, cries for help and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you, yourself, hear these noises or you were told about them?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each time, every night. Because, as I say, there was just a single wall that separated it from the room in which I was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: At any later time, did you ever meet anyone who spent time in that room?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew personally two of the persons mentioned. I had known them before coming to the camp and I met the third one then. And we met a few times after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us who they were, please.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were Jasmin Kulovac, Enver Krasic and Kadrija Sulejmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did these men ever tell you the names of anyone else who spent any time in this notorious room?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they said that Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic spent several days with them in this room, that one Mujo Hodzic spent around ten days with them and also Mujo Paraganlija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The four names you mentioned, do you know if any of them survived to leave the Rasadnik prison camp alive?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not leave the prison. The bodies of Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic were exhumed, I don't know exactly, two or three years ago in the Vragoli area. And as for Mujo Hodzic and Mujo Paraganlija are still registered as missing. Nothing is known about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did the men who did survive, you said Mr. Kulovac, Mr. Krasic, and Mr. Sulejmanovic, did they tell you anything about how the four men who didn't survive had been treated while they were in this room?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were regularly beaten while they were accommodated there. But they also don't know where they were taken. They were simply taken away from that room in the night, all of them. But where and what happened to them, this is something they also do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us about one other man, Esad Cocalic who you told us was taken out of your room one night and you had been told the next day by the guard that he had been, I think, exchanged. Do you know if that man was ever taken into this notorious room?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. When they took him from our room, no one ever saw him again, either the men who were accommodated in the notorious room or us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to a slightly later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'd ask Your Honours, there's a document -- in fact, there will be three documents for which I'm going to make this request, documents which are not on our 65 ter list. They're marked with an asterisk next to them on the exhibit list we submitted to use with Mr. Dzebo. And the first one of those that I would ask to be added to the 65 ter list is number 7403. It's a document that's been disclosed to the Defence. It's actually a similar report to the first Red Cross report we saw earlier, and it is originally published in both B/C/S and in English. And I'd ask if we could go ahead to use that. If so, it should not be broadcast for the same reasons as I stated for the first of those Red Cross documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objections? Mr. Tolimir, may I ask you again, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to greet everyone present and the witness, and I hope that this day finishes according to God's will rather than with my wishes. I have nothing against this. I would just ask the Prosecution to announce the documents in future. They can be announced and perhaps they think that we might somehow abuse this if they did not announce them. Because there are always additional documents with every witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not an objection. Therefore, leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And as I said, if we could please have that on the screen but not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And this time, I think because of the cover letter situation, if we could show page 3 in the English and page 1 in the B/C/S. We should see the corresponding pages. That looks right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, the title of the document that's just being blown up on the screen now refers to ICRC visits to Rogatica and Borike on 23rd of October and 27th of October, 1995. Where were you around those dates?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We can see the second of the paragraphs under the number 1. It describes the progress of the visit: "On 23.10, the ICRC revisited 24 detainees in Rogatica. The authority informed the delegates that three detainees escaped since the last ICRC visit and that one detainee had to be transferred to Sokolac hospital where he was visited by ICRC field nurse on 02.11.1995. The other 16 detainees, on working obligation in Borike, were revisited by ICRC delegates together with the responsible of Rogatica War Admission Camp on 26.10 at their working place." Sir, do you recall being visited while you were at Borike by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they visited us at Borike. They brought some clothes. These were winter jackets, hats, gloves, I think some pullovers, track suits, and they distributed ten packs of cigarettes per each person. With their assistance, we contacted our families against by using Red Cross messages. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did you often receive such, I suppose, luxury items, such as cigarettes while you were in the prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Red Cross visited us rarely, and we only got supplies from them. I mean supplies of cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that one prisoner was taken to hospital in Sokolac and went through some surgery involving amputation. Does this correspond with what we've just seen in this part of the Red Cross report?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Hamdija Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What about what it says here concerning the escape of three detainees. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One could presume that these would be Esad Cocalic, Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic, because only those three people were missing at the time from the list. That was the difference in the head count. As for any other prisoners, from beginning to end, none of them even tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Is it possible that any of those three, though, could have escaped?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is. If they had, they would have turned up alive somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did the staff of the prison camp ever speak about these people or speak about any escapes?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a word. I said yesterday that the deputy warden Petar Despot personally took Cocalic out of the room, and the next morning he told me that his cousin from Libya had sent money for him to be exchanged. That was the only piece of information we had regarding these three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross representatives ask you or, to your knowledge, any -- the other prisoners anything about these supposed escapees?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only about that, but on the occasion of each of their visit, they had lists of people from Zepa or from other areas. And they always asked us whether we knew anything about those people, whether anyone saw them, whether they were brought there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear from your answer, did the Red Cross then ask you about those three men who are described here as having escaped or having been told to the Red Cross they had escaped?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked us if we knew anything about the three men, because they were missing at the head count during their visits. Since we didn't know anything, there was nothing to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you or the other prisoners what you should say about those missing men, if you were asked?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told us anything, probably because we never had separate individual conversations with ICRC representatives. There were always policemen around so as to be able to follow the course of those conversations at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for this exhibit to be admitted also under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7403 shall be assigned Exhibit P2253, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask now orally to add the second of the three documents I mentioned which don't currently have a 65 ter number. This one is marked as 7405. And, again, that appears on our list of intended exhibits to use with this witness, and it's marked with the usual asterisk to indicated that that's solely with leave of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that the Defence has no objection. It will be -- leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And it's a single-page document, so ... great. If we can just see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, this is one of the lists that I showed to you when we met over the last couple of days before you started to testify. And we can see at the top that this is a document sent from the Rogatica Brigade, organ for POP and sent to the Drina Corps security department on the 28th of December 1995. And if we scroll just down to the bottom, we will see who it is sent by. The English may run onto two pages, I believe. We can see there in the signature block, it's sent by Zoran Carkic. You've told us you came across Mr. Carkic while you were in the Rasadnik prison camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday that he interviewed a number of people in the premises of the camp building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us the length of time that you spent in Rasadnik camp, which I think takes us through to January of 1996. Could you tell us about the end of your stay in the prison camp and how it was that you came to be freed eventually?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Dayton Accords were signed, it was agreed that all prisoners would be exchanged. Those of us who were in Rogatica became part of that exchange programme. That's how we were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: What was the sequence of events? When did you learn that you were going to be exchanged, and when did it actually happen?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the talks in Dayton began, our guards, the policemen, told us that it was to be one of the items in the agreement and that it was only a matter of time before it is realised. Therefore, from the beginning of the Dayton peace talks, we knew what was going to happen. We only received official information about an exchange when the ICRC visited us the last time, on the 11th of January, 1996. On that occasion, we filled out a number of questionnaires. On the 15th of January, we were transferred to the prison in Kula close to the Butmir airport in Sarajevo. On the 19th, in the evening, we were finally transferred to the airport and exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: How many people from the Rogatica -- or Rasadnik prison camp were exchanged at that time in January of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Forty-three or 44; that is to say, all those who were in the camp at the time. They were all exchanged at Kula, save for Enver Krasic who wanted to be exchanged in Gorazde because that is where his family was. He remained to be taken to Gorazde; whereas we were put on buses and taken to the Kula prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Could we scroll up to the top of the page now on screen in B/C/S and back to the beginning of the English. It is going to be looking up and down this list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at this list of names and tell us if this corresponds with the people you recall who were exchanged in 1996 with you. Please let us know when we need to scroll down the page.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could actually go down a bit further. I think the numbers -- there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This completely reflects the situation. I only want to repeat that Enver Krasic was left behind waiting to be taken to Gorazde, while we went to the prison in Kula in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll down to the bottom of the English side of the page, I think we can see there -- well, even to the next page, I am afraid. It is cut off. The text there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to another part of this document, please, back in the English, I would like to know if the witness knows anything about the person number 42, Ilijas Cuprija. What about him? Was he left behind as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He, too, was exchanged with us at Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Witness, you have just told us that you were released from the prison camp in January 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question. I don't understand so I seek clarification. Earlier on you said that after you were taken to the prison camp, you returned to Zepa for the first time on the 8th of October, 1995, and you saw that the mosque had disappeared, that your family house had been burnt down and so on. So did I miss something? Did I fail to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that particular occasion, we returned to Zepa to perform our work duties. We were taken there by the camp policemen. We had work obligation to perform for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the record, I'd like to follow up from that question of Judge Mindua for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And just ask that: The occasions you described, both when you were on work detail in Zepa, you said also that you were at Borike for work detail. These times, were you remaining under guard or were you free to come and go as you pleased?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were under guard. We were accommodated in a classroom of the old school building. The military policemen guarded the building during the night. In the morning, when we went to work, they escorted us to the location. They were also deployed around the construction site. There were three or four of them there at any time. We were constantly under guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd ask if we could just return to the bottom of this document. It's the part describing under number 43, Enver Krasic. It says after that: "Prisoners of war from Gorazde registered by the ICRC and accommodated in Rogatica." Sir, does that correspond with what you were saying about Mr. Krasic and his choice, that he wanted to be exchanged back to Gorazde rather than to Sarajevo with the rest of the group?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And having had a chance to look through this list of 43 names, are these the people who were involved with you in the exchange when you were finally released from the prison camp?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not receive the full question, as interpreted. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The 43 names that we see on this list, do they correspond with the people who were released from the Rasadnik prison camp with you in January of 1996?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask for this document to be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7405 shall be assigned Exhibit P2254. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mentioned three documents I would ask to have admitted to the 65 ter list. The final one of those three is 7404.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see an objection by the Defence. Leave is granted -- yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objection because we want to have it all admitted. However, we would like to ask the Prosecutor to disclose such documents in a timely fashion so that we can prepare rather than receiving them only once testimonies have begun. They know it would be admitted, and that's why they wait so long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, when was this disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I understand it was disclosed last week when we submitted our list of proposed exhibits for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is, indeed, quite late. We would like to ask you to disclose these -- this kind of material in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We're seeing this document now up on the screen. The heading is: "List of captured Muslim fighters." And this document is not dated. Sir, again, we looked at this document when we met over the last couple of days before your testimony. And I'd ask you if you could just look down the list. Let us know when we need to scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If we could go right to the bottom of the page, please. And the English, I think again, we need to go to a second page. Sir, tell us, who are the people on this list? Do you recognise the names?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those up to number 43, and including number 43, are those who were at Rogatica camp with me. The people from 44 to 48, I don't really know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Do those 43, to the best of your knowledge, correspond with the first list we just saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is Enver Krasic, whom we mentioned, from Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And if we see at the bottom of this list, there's a remark which says: "The first 43 are in Rogatica, and the last five in the Vlasenica MUP prison. All are registered with the ICRC." Does that correspond with your knowledge of the first 43 but not of the last five?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first 43 correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And could we just go back to the top of the page for a moment, please. And back to the beginning of the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We see the list, as I mentioned, is titled: "List of captured Muslim fighters." Were all of the 43 of you in Rogatica Muslim fighters or Bosnian Muslim Army or armed police fighters?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not all. The age doesn't tally either. On one of the lists we could see years of birth, and there were some who were born back in 1934 or 1935.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And about those people who had been in the camp but had disappeared before the time of release, including Mr. Imamovic and Mr. Hajric. Do you have any information that they were Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Imamovic, throughout the war, was commander of the Civil Protection Staff in Zepa. Mehmed Hajric, I believe, did not take part in the Army of BiH. He always had a position in civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I've finished with the document. I would ask for that to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7404 shall be assigned Exhibit P2255. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, we've spent a few hours now going through your account of the time in the camp, any other areas -- your experiences in the camp that are relevant here. I would ask about any visits by senior members of the VRS. Because you started the account by telling us that it was General Tolimir who arrived when you first came to the camp. After seeing General Tolimir, did you see any other members of the VRS, senior members of the VRS, apart from the -- any people who were at the camp on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we did not receive interpretation into Serbian. Mr. Elderkin's question was not interpreted into Serbian. Therefore, Mr. Tolimir could not hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I'll repeat it and I'll try and shorten it as well, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, apart from the time when you first arrived at the Rasadnik prison camp and saw General Tolimir there, were there any other times during your imprisonment when you saw other -- not -- General Tolimir or any other senior members of the Bosnian Serb Army? If there are, please tell us about those in your own time.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I saw General Tolimir in Zepa on that day. That was the penultimate day of evacuation. I saw Pecanac throughout the evacuation process in Zepa. I don't know what his rank was. At Boksanica, I saw Kusic who was a local commander of the Rogatica Brigade. Then in Tisca, when we were brought there, I said I saw a military policeman who took us off the bus, and I also saw General Tolimir. When we were getting into the camp building, that's when I saw them, too. During our stay in the camp, we had four or five visits by General Mladic. We also had regular visits by Kusic, the local commander. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: The four or five --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question in relation to Pecanac. Was he in a uniform or did he wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was in uniform. He actually introduced himself as Pecanac. I don't really know whether it's his true name or not. That's how he introduced himself. And he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it is just about the break time. I don't have much more to ask. In any event, I would rather give the witness time to give as full an answer as he would like. It would be simply to ask him about the visits he mentioned by General Mladic during the time in the camp. It may be better simply to take the break now and then finish off with that final question. Unless the Defence would prefer me to go a few minutes longer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is a good time for the break. And then after the break, you may continue. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Elderkin, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, you mentioned that you had, I think, four or five visits by General Mladic during your stay in the camp. I was going to ask if you would take your time now, tell us about those visits, as best you remember them.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Considering the circumstances I was in, the first contact with General Mladic makes you have an impression that are you meeting a man who is coming from a world where civilisation has not yet appeared. His entrance into the rooms where we were accommodated and his first words were, Look here, Turks, your Alija should fuck you. He won't. So I have to take care of you. Then he would condition speaking provocative words. He said, You lived fine in Zepa. You had nice houses. You organised dances, but where you used to live, I will populate some mountain goats. After that, he mentioned Budicin Potok and the 4th and 5th and 6th of June, how we had sullied our hands by jumping their column. See how nice you look and you should go roast it to your families -- as we received our children, and so on and so forth. Eventually, he said, I offered to you your Alija but he won't accept you. This is why you will stay here, to work for us. We will introduce work obligation. And in front of the facilities where we were accommodated, there used to be a cow farm before the war. There were several facilities, each of them was about 70 metres long. When you completely renovate this farm for me, then I will think whether I would release you or not. More or less, each of his visits looked and sounded like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I don't have any more questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Sir, you know now Mr. Tolimir has the right to cross-examine you. But before he commences his cross-examination, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes. You have testified that eventually you were exchanged at Sarajevo airport. After you were exchanged, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the exchange, I met with my family in Kakanj. I lived there with them for less than a month, after which we moved to Sarajevo. I lived in Sarajevo until June 1999, after which I moved to the United States where I am still residing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And you testified that one of your colleagues, I cannot remember the name, opted to go to Gorazde. You recall that? One of the people who was incarcerated with you in the prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was Enver Krasic. Everybody else from the list I mentioned were exchanged at the Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Subsequently, do you know if Enver Krasic is still alive and is still in Gorazde? Do you know? If you don't, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I never got in touch with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just one more last question. You said just now that after the exchange you went back with your family. Should I assume you went back to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I joined my wife and my children in Kakanj. As I said, I lived there for about a month and subsequently I moved to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now it's your turn to commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again I wish to greet everyone. I wish peace for this house and I hope that God's will be done in these proceedings rather than my wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also greet Mr. Dzebo. And I wish he has a plenty stay here amongst us. As we are speaking the same language, I would ask him to wait when I ask a question and say "thank you" until the transcript is recorded and then only begin with his answer. I will try to do the same. Thank you. I will start with the last questions, in order to facilitate matters for you. Judge Nyambe just asked you about Enver Krasic who said that he wished to go to Gorazde. Do you know whether he features on a list of missing persons or whether he was exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was exchanged or whether he figures on a list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nyambe also asked you about how you were exchanged at the Sarajevo airport and where did you meet with your family. Please tell us whether, on the occasion of your exchange at Sarajevo on 18th of January, 1996, General Tolimir was present and did you see him there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you need your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did General Tolimir show up at the reception centre for prisoners of war at Rasadnik near Rogatica after the 27th of July or, rather, the 28th, after he talked with you and your group at the prison? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him after that. I just remember the first day when we were brought to the camp building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were eventually asked about persons who were exchanged together with you at the Sarajevo airport and those who were from Vlasenica, the five men who were added to your list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see P2255 in e-court, which was shown to you, as it's a Prosecution document, so that you could have a look. It used to be 65 ter 7405. Thank you. Thank you. We can see the list now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see down to number 37. Can we please scroll down so that we can see down to 43. That was the number of people you said were exchanged with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please place the document so that number 43, Krasic, Enver, is in the bottom in e-court. Thank you. So that Krasic, Enver, number 43, is the last one on the list, towards the bottom of the list, so that we could see those who are above him, so that we could see the first nine that are on the list. Thank you. There it is. Thanks. We can see now the list beginning with the Camil Kulovac. Under number 1, it should say Kulovac. Down to 43 which is Enver Krasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us for the record whether these 43 persons were exchanged with you on the 18th of January, 1996, at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, all those from number 1 through to number 42, concluding with Ilijas Cuprija were transported to prison Kula at Butmir. Enver Krasic remained to wait for transportation in the direction of Gorazde because he had expressed the wish to be exchanged at the check-point in Kopaci near Gorazde. Whether he left on the very same day, whether he stayed there longer, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to ask you again something you already told the Prosecutor, for the sake of transcript, but I have to. The rule is that it should enter the transcript. This is my question: As for these 42 persons from the list, from number 1 to number 43, concluding with Ilijas Cuprija, did they cross over from the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska to the territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 18th of January, 1996, when the exchange at the Sarajevo airport took place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Tolimir, to slow down. It is difficult for the recorder to record everything you have said. And please pause between question and answer to avoid overlapping. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we can still see the list, I wish to ask you the following, Mr. Dzebo. Were all those who were together with you at the reception centre in Rasadnik in Rogatica exchanged together with you or not on the day of the exchange; that is to say, the 18th of January. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again: Everyone except Enver Krasic was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please say for the record whether all those whom you were meeting at the reception centre Rasadnik in Rogatica from the period when you arrived there to the time when you left were exchanged, and if not, who was not? Thank you. Just pause a minute before answering.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone who happened to be there at the time when I was detained was exchanged, except Mehmed Hajric, Amir Imamovic, and Esad Cocalic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please say for the record when was the last time you saw Mehmed Hajric and what was the reason he was not exchanged with you when you were exchanged? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be 100 per cent precise in terms of the date, but I think it was in mid-August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that until the 15th of August, 1995, he was at the reception centre for prisoners of war Rasadnik in Rogatica? I mean Mr. Mehmed Hajric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether you know when Amir Imamovic left the reception centre and when did you stop seeing him at the reception centre for prisoners of war at Rasadnik near Rogatica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about the same time as Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, did Amir Imamovic then go missing from the reception centre for prisoners of war at Rasadnik near Rogatica on the 15th of August, 1995, and was it then that you stopped seeing him and didn't see him after that date?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him again after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also talked about Mujo Hodzic; do you remember that? And do you know when he left the reception centre Rasadnik in Rogatica? Thank you. Do you know the day and the month, if you remember? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Mujo Hodzic, but I also noted that I didn't see Mujo personally after the exchange. I talked to people accommodated in the so-called notorious room, as we called it, and they told me that Mujo Hodzic and Mujo Paraganlija had been there. Under what circumstances they were taken away from there, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you learned from other prisoners whether they were taken away before Hajric and Amir Imamovic or were they taken away from the detention facility in Rogatica after them.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were taken away before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at 1D785.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is your statement. You can see it now. That is your statement given to the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina after your arrival from the reception centre in Rogatica. In paragraph 4, as we may call it, you say -- it's page 2 in English, please. Or it's even better to have a look first at paragraph 2 so that you would remember better. You say in paragraph 2: "The first time we could wash ..." Did you find this?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see page 1 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at page 4 of your statement, paragraph 2 in the Serbian language, which is page 4 also in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here it is. The easiest way to notice it is where it says "the 6th of August, 1995, "in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's line 7, and you say the following: "On 6th of August, 1995, in Rakitnica river, was the first time we were allowed to wash and the next time was seven days later," in the Rakitnica river. "In this interfering period, effendi Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic disappeared from the camp. From then on, we heard cries coming from the so-called infamous room every day. We heard different cries and orders to get up. I was later told by Jasmin Kulovac that Mehmed Hajric and Amir Imamovic had been taken to this room and that they had been tortured and beaten there day and night for about ten days. One early evening after ten days, they were taken away, and we ... never learned what ... happened to them. Following their disappearance, Mujo Hodzic from the village of Osva [phoen], Rogatica municipality, was taken to this infamous room. He, too, spent about ten days there, and he, too, was beaten and tortured non-stop. We could hear his moans and cries. He, too, disappeared; he was taken away? "In mid-August, they started taking us and the wounded to labour," so on. This is my question: Can one see from this part of your statement that Mr. Mujo Hodzic arrived after the 15th of August to the so-called infamous room; that is to say, after the departure or disappearance, as you called it, of Mr. Mehmed Hajric and Mr. Amir Imamovic? Does this description correspond to that, this part of your statement, I mean? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I said in the statement, or, rather, in the part of the statement is something that is -- that was retold to me by Jasmin Kulovac. I repeat, as I said yesterday, throughout this period, we heard beatings, we heard cries but we didn't know who that was. I learned this from Jasmin only once the exchange had taken place. It was quite normal that everything was being discussed and so this was one of the things that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzebo. Can you please tell us whether then Jasmin Kulovac, Enver, and Kadrija Sejmen [as interpreted], who were also in the room and who were exchanged with you, should they know when Hajric, Imamovic, and now this Mujo Hodzic we are talking about, left the room and then later on also Mujo Paraganlija. So could they help us to conclude who disappeared from the detention facility at what time? Can you help the Trial Chamber? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably one of these three or all three of them would be much more precise than me in terms of this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would kindly ask you to repeat two names. At the beginning of your last question, you said: "Can you please tell us whether then Jasmin Kulovac," and then you mentioned two other names which were not recorded. Could you please repeat these names, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I mentioned Kadrija Sulejmanovic, and I mentioned Enver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now the witness, Mr. Dzebo, can tell us what was his actual name for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was Enver Krasic and Kadrija Sulejmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzebo. Can we please just say briefly for the sake of the record, are there witnesses who saw when Mr. Hajric, Mehmed; Amir Imamovic; Mujo Hodzic and Mujo Paraganlija were taken from the reception centre for prisoners of war in Rasadnik near Rogatica? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three of those who were in the room and who have been mentioned can be witnesses who would be more precise than myself. As I said previously, they are Jasmin Kulovac, Kadrija Sulejmanovic, and Enver Krasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now please look at the very same page we are looking at now. And below the passage I read out to you from, the following paragraph says: "In mid-August" -- I'm quoting your statement now: "In mid-August, they started taking us and the wounded to labour. This involved clearing out the stables, cutting wood, digging canals," and so on. "On the 5th of September, 1995, at about 2245 hours, the deputy camp warden, Mr. Petar Despot, also known as Pero, came into my room and took out Esad Cocalic from the village of Stitari, Visegrad municipality. In the morning, Pero told us that Esad Cocalic had been taken to be exchanged. And then follows what we said during examination-in-chief about his brother from Libya. This is my question: The 5th [Realtime transcript read in error "35th"] of September, 1995, was that the date when Esad Cocalic went missing from the reception centre for prisoners of war at Rasadnik near Rogatica where you were also detained at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that date, in the evening, Mr. Petar Despot, who was deputy prison warden, took him out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I think it may be unnecessary, but since it is staring out in the last paragraph, "the 35th of September." Clearly corresponds to the 5th of September that was referred to in the quotation previously. But ... we should probably make a note that the 35th of September is an incorrect reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since there is never a 35th of September, I think you are quite correct, looking at the document on the screen. Please continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you, Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Dzebo, can you tell us whether you know if any other detainees who were with you in the reception centre Rasadnik in Rogatica, went missing while you were there as a POW in 1995 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such cases. I believe they were all exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are discussing your statement, let's look at page 5, paragraph -- well, we may call it 4, line 6. You mention Budicin Potok. During examination-in-chief, you said that you were interrogated in August 1995 about certain events in Budicin Potok. Can you tell the Chamber, since they are not familiar with the name of Budicin Potok, what it was all about? What events did you refer to when you said you were interrogated in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't want to talk much about Budicin Potok because it is well known that it took place between the 5th -- 4th and the 6th of June, 1992. I arrived in the territory of Zepa on the 21st of July; that is to say, a month and a half later. All I can say is -- is what I heard from others. I don't know how balanced those stories were or whether things were blown out of proportion or not. It is known that there was a column of JNA vehicles transporting either JNA regulars or reserve soldiers heading for the Zlovrh facility, which used to be a JNA facility. En route to Budicin Potok, they burned some houses in the village of Stoborani as well as in the village of Godenje. In the hamlet of Luke, a few kilometres before, they encountered some obstacles on the road. They did the same. So there were obstacles on the road at Budicin Potok.
